turn_text: In just a few days we'll come up on the fifth round of renegotiation of the North American Free Trade Agreement and just a few days ago, you took this issue to the Trade Representative and asking for some assurances. How do you see these NAFTA talks and what are threats of the administration of just pulling out a NAFTA and pulling out a chorus?

Well, that would be disastrous. And I didn't just talk to Lighthouse there. I actually also had a chance to speak with Commerce Secretary with Wilbur Ross, where I just, maybe because he had made some comments that I disagreed with and I just wanted to impress upon him how critically important that trading agreement is to North Dakota. and to the rest of agriculture. And I know that Secretary Perdue is our greatest advocate, but they need to hear from people on the Hill that there will be a level of unhappiness. If we do anything more, that results in damaged relationships between us and our two greatest agricultural trading partners for North Dakota's interest in that's Canada and Mexico.
The President has talked about using bilateral trade agreements to replace what would have been agreements under the Trans-Pacific Partnership. We've been better off with TPP.

You want my informed opinion, the answer is yes. However, when I met with Lighthizer before the ambassador was confirmed, you know, he made an impassioned argument to me about bilaterals and I said, well, you know, I sure hope you're right. I'm very concerned about backing away from TPP, very concerned about that agreement going forward, very concerned about our trading partners looking to other markets, and that would be devastating for agriculture. And I think that you now see all the commodity groups, you see the trade groups the agricultural trade group standing up saying, whoa, whoa, whoa, do no harm. That was one of the founding principles for renegotiation of NAFTA. turn_text: One of the big items that is ahead of both the House and the Senate is likely tax reform. What do you feel has to be changed to the current tax code to support agriculture? And what needs to be left alone?

Well, interest deduction for farmers needs to be left alone. I'll put that kind of front row and center. You know, a lot of our farmers enjoy expensing already with 179. And so, you know, any kind of trade off there, or perceived trade off there, needs to be wholly examined. We have a really interesting situation in North Dakota. We don't allow sea corpse to farm, so that any kind of sea-corp release that would be given to farmers in other jurisdictions, isn't available in North Dakota. And so we need to make sure that we're leveling the playing field. We need to make sure that we again do no harm, that we don't actually increase costs for our farmers in these very precarious times. And so we're reading through all of this with a fine-toothed comb. One of the challenges that we have to confront is take a look at estate tax removal. There's a lot of talk about eliminating the estate tax. If it's done at the expense of stepped up basis, that's going to be a huge problem. We also have a problem with 199 as it relates to our co-ops. And so we're hearing from the farm groups now. We're continuing to have a dialogue. They'll meet with Gary Cohen. A number of Democrats are going over and having a discussion with him about tax reform. We're going to take some of these challenges and some of these issues directly to them.
